Joining their palms toward the Buddha and gazing at him without weariness, not casting their eyes away for even a moment—this is the karma of the body (*kāyakarman*). It continues...
That their eyes, having already rejoiced, each praised the merits of the Tathāgata is the vocal action (*vāk-karman*).

Reaching the limit of what can be seen by the physical eye is called "beyond the range of the eye. They rejoice because they have been blessed with the benefit of the Dharma; because they rejoice, they offer praise.
Since each person praises individually, it is said "each and every one. To be fully endowed with mindfulness of the Buddha is the mental action (*manas-karman*) directed toward the Buddha.
The physical body and all its merits are entirely held in mind; therefore, it is said that they are "fully endowed. In the third section, regarding her returning to the city:
this refers to the skillful means of propagating the teaching. While Śrīmālā resided in the palace, she was separated from the king by another city; now, she wishes to transform the king.
One must go to the king’s residence; therefore, she enters the city and praises the Mahāyāna by extolling the king to her friends.
She converts the king first because he is the sovereign of the nation; wishing now to lead the common people together with him, she converts him first.
Among the women in the city, Queen Śrīmālā and others convert them according to their respective categories. In the fourth section, there are four distinct parts. First:
The Buddha entered the Jeta Grove and instructed Ānanda regarding what was to be entrusted. Twice, Śakra, Lord of Devas, descended, and that which was entrusted arrived in both instances.

A third time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, descended; the Buddha preached the sūtra for him and entrusted the Dharma to him. A fourth time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, along with Ānanda and the great assembly, descended;
this clarifies how the entire multitude heard the Dharma and joyfully practiced it. Regarding the first section, the Tathāgata first physically entered [the grove].
At Jetavana, the Buddha next addressed Ānanda with his own voice; because Ānanda was in his immediate presence, he spoke to him directly.
Subsequently, he called upon Śakra with his mind; since Śakra was at a distance, the Buddha summoned him through mental intent.

"Śakra" is a term from the language of the Hu (Indians); it refers to the Lord of Devas. "Śakra" means "capable. Because he is capable of being the Lord of Devas, he is named Śakra-devānām-indra. This concludes the second section.
As for the sudden arrival of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, at that time: because their holy minds were in mutual resonance, when the Buddha thought of him, Śakra immediately arrived.
Since Ānanda was already there, he is not mentioned [in this context]. In the third section, he first expounds the sutra;

having finished speaking, he issues the following entrustment of the Dharma. First, he entrusts it generally to both Śakra and Ānanda; then, from "Furthermore, Kauśika... onwards, he entrusts it specifically.

Entrustment to Śakra. This section contains two parts: first, praising the benefits and exhorting to uphold; second, Śakra’s inquiry as to what the name of this teaching should be, which constitutes the specific instruction for upholding.
Within the praise of benefits and exhortation, there is first the entrustment to Śakra, followed by the entrustment to Ānanda.
Regarding the entrustment to Śakra: "You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra. This is a direct exhortation to uphold it. [Regarding] men and women...
"Like the sands of the Ganges," and so forth, praises the benefits and exhorts one to uphold [the teaching]. "Therefore," and so forth, concludes with an exhortation to receive and uphold it.
Within the section praising the benefits and exhorting, the term "Kauśika" is used to address the recipient of this entrustment. This Kauśika is a specific name for Śakra.
As Nāgārjuna has stated, in a past age, there was a Brahmin in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī whose family name was Kauśika; he was intelligent and wise.

Possessing great wisdom, he practiced meritorious deeds together with thirty-two of his peers. At the end of his life, among the Kauśikas, he attained the status of a celestial lord (*devendra*), while the other thirty-two all became his ministers.
The Buddha, knowing this matter from its origin, addressed him by the name Kauśika.
Having cultivated the practices for enlightenment and the six *pāramitās* throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [the Buddha] mentions the inferior to manifest the superior.
If one were to compare the merit of hearing and receiving [the teachings], up to the point of holding the sutra, with that of others, the former would be superior and the latter inferior.

This refers to practicing the six *pāramitās* by grasping at signs within the Mahayana teachings of provisional transformation, while remaining ignorant of this teaching that reveals the ultimate reality.
Within this sutra, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is revealed and elucidated; [therefore,] hearing, reciting, and even holding this sutra [yields far greater merit].
Because it reveals the nature of the treasury, the merit of one who listens to, receives, reads, recites, and upholds [this teaching] is greater than that [of the former].
This "upholding" refers to delighting in and loving the sutra, desiring to open it, and not merely seeking its principles in a superficial manner; the merit of such upholding is greater than that.

How much more so for one who explains it to others? Using the inferior to illustrate the superior: if upholding it oneself yields such great merit, how much more so when speaking it for others. Therefore...
The following section concludes with an exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching]. Regarding the statement "spoken for the thirty-three gods":
within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are thirty-three distinct abodes. The residence of Śakra is counted as one side;
because the residences of each of his eight ministers are distinct, there are thirty-three separate divisions. Since these are all places ruled by Śakra, he is exhorted [to uphold it].

It was preached for their sake and subsequently entrusted to Ānanda; its characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood. Within the second section, which lists the names and instructs on upholding [the teaching], first, Śakra requests:
"What shall this sutra be named? This asks for the name of the sutra. Then, "How should it be upheld? asks for the manner of upholding it.

The Buddha answers this in three distinct sections. First, the statement that "this sutra accomplishes immeasurable merit and cannot be fully observed or known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" demonstrates the vastness of this Dharma;
it is called "incapable of being exhausted. Second, from "Kauśika" onwards, it reveals the profundity of this Dharma;
it is called "incapable of being fathomed. Third, from "Now, furthermore" onwards, it relies upon its essential summary.
The listing of names for instruction and upholding: herein, first, there is the empowerment and permission to speak. Then, Śakra, Lord of Devas, descends to respectfully receive the teaching.
Following the Buddha’s words, the names are listed for instruction and upholding. Within each chapter, the name is first listed in response to the initial question;
subsequently, the instruction for receiving and upholding follows in response to the latter question. This praises the Tathāgata’s true virtues. This is...

Regarding the "Former Tathāgata’s Wondrous Form Body" and so forth: to maintain these names in this manner, guarding them with diligence so as not to lose them, is called "receiving and maintaining" (*udgrahaṇa*).
Subsequent categories are similar. Not contemplating the "Great Receiving" refers to the aforementioned reverence.

The "Receiving of the Ten Receptions" and so forth encompasses all vows; this refers to the aforementioned Śrīmālā, who again before the Buddha made the three vows and so forth—not contemplating [them].

"Acceptance" refers to what was previously stated by the Buddha regarding discipline (*vinaya*) and so forth, which explains the entry into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is the aforementioned passage where the Buddha told [the interlocutor]:
"Now I shall further explain for you the acceptance of the Dharma taught by all Buddhas, namely, the infinite Noble Truths. This occurs within the preceding section of the text.

The initial contemplation on the Truths (*satya*) and so forth explains the *tathāgatagarbha*. This refers to the profound meaning and other points explained previously in the section concerning the noble king (*rājārya*).

Regarding the explanation of the *dharmakāya*: this refers to the previous passage stating that if one has no doubt regarding being enshrouded by immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*), one likewise has no doubt regarding the *dharmakāya* that emerges from those afflictions;
thus, the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is concealed. This refers to the aforementioned passage where the wisdom of the *tathāgatagarbha* is [the subject].

Regarding the "knowledge of emptiness" and so forth: those who speak of a single truth refer to these four [truths] mentioned above; three are impermanent, and one is permanent, and so on. Regarding the "single reliance":
among the four worldly dharmas mentioned previously, one relies upon that which transcends the world (*lokottara*), and so forth.
As for "inversion and reality," within the preceding text it says: "The *tathāgatagarbha* is not the self (*ātman*), not a living being (*jīva*), and not a life-principle (*jantu*)."
The phrase "human beings and others" refers to those whose pure nature is obscured. The term "Tathāgatagarbha" mentioned in the preceding text refers to the "Dharmadhātugarbha" and so forth.
The expression "true children" refers to those previously described as "those who follow faith" and "those with increased faith," and so on.

The "lion’s roar of Queen Śrīmālā" refers to what was further explained in the preceding text for the sake of additional benefit. From here below, the second section follows, which specifically entrusts [the teaching].
As for Śakra, because he was a layperson living at home, it was feared that he might not keep this in mind; therefore, the Buddha entrusted it to him separately.
Furthermore, because Śakra would live for a long time until the arrival of the Final Dharma (mappō), the Buddha entrusted it to him specifically. First, he praised the excellence of the sutra.

Next, regarding the entrustment: as for the duration of the Dharma’s abiding, it is stated that the True Dharma of Śākyamuni shall last for five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma for a thousand years, and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years. During this time, you should read, recite, and extensively expound it for others.

Below the words "Śakra addressed [the Buddha]," it says: "I respectfully accept the instruction to transmit and uphold [it]. Fourth, the Great Assembly hears the Dharma and practices virtuous conduct accordingly.
Manifestly understandable.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-artha-ṭīkā*, Scroll Lower. Compiled by Shi Huiyuan.
The fifth day of the eighth month, the ninth year of the Daye era of the Great Sui.
The śramaṇa Tánjiǎo transcribed this for circulation in future generations.
This concludes the collation. End of Volume II of the Commentary on the Sūtra.
